floss-rs: FLOSS, ported to Rust, emulating with icicle

verdict: it works floss tests 43/43 69–109× faster (median) MIT/Apache-2.0 stack x86 · x64 · PE · shellcode

Can FLOSS, the FLARE Obfuscated String Solver, run on a fast, permissively licensed emulator instead of vivisect's pure-Python one? Yes. This page shows what was built, how it works, how it compares with Python FLOSS on real malware, and where icicle falls short.

the question

FLOSS finds strings that malware hides: strings built on the stack one character at a time, strings decoded in place by tight loops, and strings produced by decoding routines. It finds them by emulating the program's code and looking at what the code writes to memory. FLOSS emulates with vivisect, which is written in pure Python, and spends almost all its time there. On the 40 malware samples in this study, Python FLOSS averaged 228 seconds per file and took up to 20 minutes.

Unicorn, the usual fast emulator, is GPL-3, which rules it out. The goal was to find out whether a permissively licensed emulator could do FLOSS's job. Three questions:

  • does icicle support what FLOSS needs: exploring every path of a function with snapshots at branches, ignoring faults and invalid memory, running decoders many times from different call contexts, following loops, and diffing memory;
  • can the result be understood and maintained, without special cases;
  • does it work on FLOSS's tests, on capa's test files, and on real malware.

the verdict

summary

icicle is a good fit. floss-rs passes every FLOSS test case, including one Python FLOSS marks as an expected failure. On real malware it finds the strings Python FLOSS finds, and nearly twice as many novel strings, 69–109 times faster. icicle's x86 semantics match Unicorn's (QEMU's) on 99.91% of instructions sampled from real malware. The remaining gaps are known and small, and none of them blocks the port.

The speed changes what FLOSS can afford to do. Python FLOSS emulates the 20 highest-scoring candidate decoding routines because each one costs seconds, and those 20 find only about 40% of what emulating every candidate finds. floss-rs emulates the 20, then keeps going down the ranking on every CPU until it has spent 5 seconds, and tells the user it is doing so. That finds 99.5% of what emulating everything finds, at a mean of 2 seconds per file. How that default was chosen is a study of its own.

architecture

Each layer only knows about the layers below it. Each analysis is short: a strategy for running code, an observer that decides when to look at memory, and a rule for which strings to report.

the emulator: icicle in a forgiving address space

floss-rs uses icicle as an instruction-semantics engine. It executes one instruction at a time and keeps memory layout, calls, APIs, and snapshots under its own control. FLOSS emulates code out of context, starting from some function with garbage arguments and no process around it. So the address space is built to keep code running rather than to be faithful:

  • the image: each section is mapped read/write, and executable if it is in the PE;
  • the stack: 512KB filled with 0xFE, with the stack pointer in the middle, so code can read its "arguments";
  • the heap: a bump allocator for the API models;
  • the void: every other address. Reads return 0xFE and writes are discarded. This is an icicle I/O memory region, so wild pointers never stop emulation and never allocate memory. vivisect behaves the same way under FLOSS.

Imports are stubs. Each import table entry points to an address in the void that decodes as a pseudo-instruction. Executing it runs the API's model (if there is one), pops the return address and any stdcall arguments, and sets the return value. It doesn't matter how the program gets there: call [IAT], a thunk, a pointer from GetProcAddress, or a pushed return address. Observers see API calls as instructions, so they can look at memory right before an API runs.

Snapshots are copy-on-write. In vivisect, a snapshot is a deep copy of all memory, and that is the main reason FLOSS is slow. icicle shares pages with the running emulator until they are written. floss-rs adds a compact register snapshot (icicle's own copies a 128KB register file), so snapshot plus restore costs about 4µs. Diffs between two views skip pages that are still shared and can be computed incrementally.

three ways to run code

driverwhat it doesused forviv-utils equivalent
exploreevery path through a function, each instruction once. Snapshots at each conditional branch, queues both sides breadth-first, steps over calls.stack strings, finding call contextsFullCoverageEmulatorDriver
explore_toexplore until an address is reached; leave the emulator therereaching a tight loopSinglePathEmulatorDriver
run_tofollow the one concrete path, into calls, with budgets for instructions and visits per addressrunning loops and decodersDebuggerEmulatorDriver

the analyses

  • stack strings: explore each function. At each call, and at the end of each block with five or more movs to memory, look for strings between the stack pointer and the initial stack pointer. Global memory is diffed at the same points.
  • tight strings: for each tight loop, explore to it, snapshot memory, run to the block after the loop, and report what the loop wrote.
  • decoded strings: rank candidate decoding routines using FLOSS's features, feature for feature. Explore each caller and snapshot at each call to the candidate. Run from each context to the return address, viewing memory before each call to an API that isn't modeled, and at the end. Report the strings that overlap changed memory.

improvements over FLOSS

The goal was more and better strings, not output identical to Python FLOSS. Each change below fixes something Python FLOSS gets wrong or can't afford:

changewhy
report whole strings that overlap changed memory, not only the changed bytesFLOSS misses UTF-16 decoded into zeroed buffers (the zero high bytes don't change), fragments strings decoded in place, and reports pieces like hell and o world
report each decoded string once per routine, even when its neighboring bytes differ between callsleftovers in a reused buffer made one string come out once per call context (54 copies of one key in one sample)
a string that grows across views is reported once, finisheda decoder that calls an API after each character produced every prefix of the string
diff global memory during stack string extraction; diff all memory around tight loopsstrings built or decoded into globals and the heap
emulate candidate routines that nothing calls from their entry pointexports, callbacks, and entry points with inlined decoders
count calls to a thunk as calls to its targetan optimized x64 decoder that starts with a jump into its rotated loop looks like a thunk
time budget: the top 20 candidates, then more, on every CPU, until 5s are spentFLOSS's top 20 find about 40% of the strings; the budget finds 99.5% (details)
API models match exact namesFLOSS matches by substring, so free catches FreeLibrary, and _vsnprintf "decodes" every format string
filter the emulator's own artifacts in more formsthe fill byte as fefe:fefe:… or 0xFEFEFEFEFEFEFEFE in decimal, and pieces of the emulated module path
tried and rejected

Trimming each reported string to only the characters that changed removed leftover junk. It also cut the last y off Conti's cmd.exe /c net stop W3Svc /y commands, and the 9 off a base64 alphabet. Conti builds the ciphertext on the stack and decodes it in place, and characters the cipher leaves unchanged look exactly like leftovers. Losing characters from real strings is worse than reporting junk, so per-routine deduplication replaced trimming.

what only floss-rs reports

Complete net stop service lists, antivirus driver names (avipbb.sys, cmdhlp.sys), Task Scheduler and registry configuration keys, cryptocurrency wallet paths, and key material. There is also noise: format strings filled in with garbage, intermediate states of decoders (w1X1_1\1V1C1), and crypto tables built at run time. how long to emulate decoding routines

FLOSS emulates the 20 highest-scoring candidate decoding routines (plus tight functions), a limit set by Python's speed. floss-rs can afford far more, so the question is how many to emulate, and how to decide without asking the user.

method288 native capa files · 170k candidate routines
data

Every candidate of every file was emulated, recording each routine's time and strings. Routines are emulated independently, so any stopping rule can be replayed offline from this one run: its value is the union of the strings from the routines it would run, its cost the sum of their times.

what counts

novel: not in the file as-is, and not mostly static text from the file (which drops format strings filled in with garbage). meaningful: novel, at least 6 characters, mostly letters, not repetitive. The measure is the share of each file's strings found, averaged over files, so one file can't dominate.

checks

Rules were tuned on half of the files and checked on the other half. The chosen default was then run for real and scored against emulating everything.

two performance bugs, found along the way

The slowest 1% of routines took 59% of all decoding time, up to 36 seconds for one routine, and almost never found anything. One cause was memory diffing: with a view before every unmodeled API call, a routine that had written megabytes compared them all at each of thousands of calls. The other was the memcpy and memset models with garbage sizes, copying megabytes of fill bytes into the void 16 bytes at a time. Both are fixed, with identical output. Emulating every candidate of every file now takes 622 seconds, where before it took 1,154 seconds and four files hadn't finished at 60 seconds each. The slowest routine now takes 5 seconds.

where the strings come from

share of meaningful strings, by the candidate's rank

FLOSS's score ranks candidates only a little better than random: at a 2 second budget, 87% against 79%. An ideal order, known only in hindsight, would find every string within half a second per file. The routines that decode strings are few and cheap but hard to spot, which led to a better ranking. The numbers in this section use FLOSS's ranking.

so

No signal beat simply spending the time, so the budget stays a plain time limit that the user doesn't need to tune. The improvements are in how much work fits inside it: the two performance fixes, and several threads. The default is now 5 seconds on every CPU. It finds 99.5% of what emulating every candidate finds, and its mean time per file matches the old 2 second, single-thread default. Given the same candidates, the output doesn't depend on the number of threads. When the budget stops early, floss-rs says so and how to go further, and --time-budget 0 reproduces FLOSS's fixed set.

Across the corpus, the default finds 2.4 times the novel strings of FLOSS's fixed set, and twice the meaningful ones. Examples include ransom note text, a Monero wallet registry key, a Bitcoin wallet.dat path, the root\SecurityCenter2 WMI namespace, and DNS-over-HTTPS queries. 45% of the added strings are meaningful; the rest are noise like Runtime error 254 at 00452E57, which is the next thing to work on.

ranking candidates

Which candidates come first decides what FLOSS finds with its top 20, and what floss-rs finds before its time budget runs out. FLOSS ranks them by a weighted average of features: block and instruction counts, arguments, callers, loops, and one feature for every non-zeroing xor, shift and mov through a register. With the top 20, that finds 39% of the text-like strings that emulating every candidate finds. floss-rs computes the score as FLOSS does; it differs from Python FLOSS's only where vivisect and lancelot see slightly different code.

what actually decodes strings
  • coordinators: big functions with many calls, often called by nothing (entry points, thread routines). Emulating one runs the decoders it calls, once per string. FLOSS ranked one of these 161st of 203; it finds 11 of its file's 12 strings.
  • decoders: small functions called from many places, often with buffers on the caller's stack, or one small function per string (Conti: 26–43 instructions with a loop over bytes, for each string).
  • meanwhile FLOSS's top-ranked functions are often unrolled hashing or crypto with hundreds of xors, which find nothing: the average over every xor and mov puts them first.

The right 20 candidates would find 99% of each file's strings, and most strings are found by just one routine, so the question is how to spot those routines in advance.

features tried

A feature dump (examples/candidate_features) computed about 40 features per candidate. It covers FLOSS's own, plus what the callers pass (pointers to data, text, zeros or the stack; small constants), whether the result goes to an API, calls out, what the function reaches through its calls, and what its loops do. Each was joined with what the routine found when emulated. To keep junk like fUAMwBEIszZgD from counting, strings were also checked against a character-trigram model of the corpus's static strings (text-like).

featureAUC within files
instructions0.71

instructions in loops; calls to functions with loops0.66
calls out; byte accesses in loops0.65
FLOSS's score0.63
what callers pass, what's done with the result0.50–0.56

The call-site features, which looked the most promising, predict almost nothing. Size predicts best, because emulating a function runs the code it calls. Changing FLOSS's formula to count each kind of feature once, instead of once per instruction, made it worse: those per-instruction counts were acting as a measure of size.

A boosted model over every feature does best with the top 20, but no better within a time budget, and it's a black box of 200 trees. A linear score fitted to half the files did better on that half and worse on the other. The two-feature score wasn't fitted at all and gets most of the gain. It beats FLOSS's score on both halves of the files, and for every kind of string, by 3–16 points with the top 20. Its top 20 take no longer to emulate.

for python FLOSSscripts/budget/floss-size-score.patch

The same change for FLOSS, in identify.py and features/extract.py, about 50 lines. It ranks candidates by the new score and keeps the old one as weighted_score. FLOSS never emulates functions that nothing calls, so in a replay of FLOSS's setting those find nothing. There, the new score (among called functions) finds 53% of the text-like strings with the top 20, where FLOSS's score finds 38%.

Python FLOSS with the patch, on the 40-file subset: 288 text-like decoded strings where it found 272, and 21% of the all-candidates run's text-like strings per file where it found 11%. 35 files are unchanged, 4 gain and 1 loses. The 3 strings only the old score finds are junk (Jmountain, Jmounta#$, mountain). The 19 only the new score finds include Iphlpapi.dll, Rstrtmgr.dll, RmShutdown, API names and a Conti net stop command. That's a real gain, but a small one on this subset.

icicle: fit, accuracy, gaps

FLOSS needsicicle
x86 and x64 user-mode instruction semanticsSLEIGH specs: Ghidra's, with pending fixes, from open_sleigh; see the differential testing below
execute one instruction at a time, inspect state betweenVm::step(1), about 0.2µs
save and restore state, cheaply, many timescopy-on-write memory snapshots, about 2µs; floss-rs copies only the register slots in use
compare memory before and aftersnapshots expose their pages, so shared pages are skipped
keep going after wild memory accessesan I/O memory region over unused address space
handle faults and keep exploring other pathsfaults are exits with a code and an address
a permissive license; no Ghidra installationMIT/Apache-2.0; the specs (2.3MB) are embedded, and compiled from memory at startup in about 0.3s

differential testing against Unicorn

124k unique instructions were collected from 60 capa test files, giving 248k cases, each with random registers, flags, and SSE registers. Each case ran on icicle and on Unicorn (used only as a test oracle), and registers, flags (including AF), SSE state, and memory were compared. Of the 186,338 cases that ran on both, 186,184 match (99.94%). The specs come from open_sleigh, pinned in June 2026: Ghidra 12.1's x86, plus upstream fixes still in review and icicle's own patches. Compared with Ghidra's latest x86, they fix xchg, psraw, cpuid, and the AF flag, and break the parity flag of daa/das; strings found in the capa corpus are the same.

differencecasesmatters for FLOSS?
div/idiv don't raise #DE on quotient overflow68no
pcmpistri, sysret unimplemented16rarely: pcmpistri is in optimized strlen
cvttsd2si/cvttss2si saturate instead of returning "integer indefinite"10no
MXCSR starts at 0, not 0x1f8014no: floss-rs sets it
daa/das set the parity flag wrong7no

performance

  • lifting dominates. Decoding and lifting an instruction with SLEIGH costs several µs, and about 30µs with icicle's lift-time optimizer on. FLOSS runs most code once, so floss-rs turns off the optimizer and the JIT, which makes it 3–7× faster on larger files.
  • per instruction, exploring every function: 7.5–10.6µs cold, 2.4–3.7µs with lifted code cached. vivisect takes 1,541µs on the same exploration, so floss-rs is about 170× faster.

gaps and workarounds

gapworkaround in floss-rsfixable in icicle
self-modifying code: writes to lifted code fault, and the disassembly cache survives snapshot restoresflush the code cache and retryyes: make the check optional
CPU snapshots copy a 128KB register filecopy the slots in useyes
user-ops without implementations (AVX, SSE4.2 string ops, AES, some x87)implement pshufb; xgetbv reports no AVX, so C runtime code takes non-AVX pathsyes, or in SLEIGH
hlt loops forever (Ghidra's semantics)treat it as a trap—
stepping off a breakpoint doesn't advanceuse step(1), no breakpoints—
the VM is built from spec files on diskcompile the embedded specs from memory, and set up the VM the same wayyes: take the files' contents

alternatives considered

There is no other mature, permissively licensed x86 emulator library. Unicorn and Qiling are GPL and Bochs is LGPL. Triton (Apache-2.0) is a C++ symbolic execution framework. Ghidra's own p-code emulators are Java, or C++ inside the decompiler library. zyemu (MIT) is early, and lancelot's own emulator is a prototype that handles 14 mnemonics. Writing x86 semantics by hand is a large, ongoing job that SLEIGH has already done.

not done yet

  • ELF and Mach-O: lancelot loads PE, COFF, and shellcode only.
  • language-specific strings (Go, Rust), FLOSS's string tags, text and HTML rendering, result caching. None of these involve emulation.
  • return address repair: FLOSS recovers when a decoder returns to an unexpected address; floss-rs doesn't.
  • noise in decoded strings: emulating more candidates also finds more format strings filled in with garbage. Strings that are mostly static text from the file could be filtered or ranked lower; the evaluation scripts already detect them.
  • FLIRT: FLOSS's signatures are built in, but opt-in (--flirt), since loading them costs about 5s.
  • a keep-going mode: keep emulating candidates until the user presses enter. On the two largest files, the default covers only 4–15% of the candidates.

The browser build is the same code as the command line. On 10 capa test files it gives identical results, at about half the speed of the native build on one thread.

  
    
    
  • no JIT. icicle's VM always creates a JIT, which writes executable machine code, and a browser doesn't allow that. floss-rs never enables the JIT, so the browser build swaps in a stub with the same interface, through a Cargo patch, without changing icicle.
    • 
    
  • WASI, for a clock. icicle reads the clock, which the standard library supports in WebAssembly only through WASI. The module imports six WASI functions, such as the clock and randomness, and 70 lines of JavaScript provide them.
    • 
    
  • one thread, in a web worker, so the page stays responsive. More threads would need shared memory, which needs special server headers.
    • 
    
  • what's not included: the FLIRT signatures (15MB).
    • 
  


  

    
setup: Python FLOSS v4.0.0a2 with vivisect 1.3.2, no FLIRT signatures, cache disabled · floss-rs release build, defaults unless noted · 4 cores, 15GB RAM, one process at a time per run
